Left out: he shou wu and sophora (strong herbs with safety questions), thuja (can irritate), and goji, reishi and woad (no added benefit in a rinse-off). Method: in a heat-proof bowl over simmering water, warm the SCI, CAPB and cetearyl alcohol, stirring, until it's a soft dough (about 10 minutes). Off the heat, stir in the shea, olive oil, glycerin and panthenol, then the powders and tea tree. Press firmly into a silicone mould, leave 48 hours, then unmould. Makes 1 bar of about 100 g. To use: wet hair, rub the bar between your hands or in a mesh bag, massage the lather into your scalp for 1 to 2 minutes, then rinse. Keep it dry between uses so it lasts. Wear a mask while weighing SCI; the powder makes you sneeze.

name: Saebom scalp bar, full herb list (closest match)
claim: All 12 listed botanicals with olive, coconut, shea and tea tree
note: A closer copy of Saebom's listed formula: every herb on the label plus the olive, coconut, shea and tea tree it's "pressed with". Saebom doesn't show its main cleanser on that panel; this uses SCI, a gentle sulfate-free one, so it still matches "0 sulfates". He shou wu, sophora root and thuja are kept, but at tiny amounts, because they're strong. Patch test first, and use the gentler bar if your scalp is sensitive. Fermenting the herbs (Saebom's claim) isn't needed in a shampoo you rinse off after 2 minutes. Grind all the herbs to a fine powder and sieve. Same method: warm the SCI, CAPB and cetearyl alcohol over simmering water until doughy, then stir in the butters, oils and glycerin off the heat, then the powders and tea tree. Press into a mould, unmould after 48 hours, and let it harden a week. Makes about 120 g, the size of the original.

name: Easy herbal shampoo bar (melt and pour, Saebom-style)
claim: Same idea, no special cleansers to buy
note: The beginner version: cut the shampoo bar base into cubes and melt gently in a water bath. Off the heat, stir in the oil, the finely ground powders and the tea tree, pour into a mould and let it set overnight. Grind herbs to a fine powder and sieve them so no bits stick in your hair. Use it like the bar above.

name: Cashmere Mist-style perfume oil (Donna Karan dupe)
claim: Soft, clean skin scent: lily, jasmine, sandalwood and musk
note: Cashmere Mist is by Donna Karan (DKNY), not Victoria's Secret. Its notes: lily of the valley and bergamot on top, jasmine and sandalwood in the middle, ambergris and white musks at the base. Lily of the valley and musk have no natural oils, so they come from skin-safe fragrance oils; ambergris is swapped for a drop of vanilla, which adds the soft amber warmth. Bergamot FCF won't burn skin in sunlight. Add the oils to a 10 ml roller bottle, top up with jojoba, shake, and let it rest 3 to 7 days so the scent blends. Roll on pulse points. Patch test first. If you want the Victoria's Secret one, Bare Vanilla Cashmere, use the vanilla musk version instead.

name: Vanilla cashmere perfume oil (like Victoria's Secret Bare Vanilla Cashmere)
claim: Creamy vanilla wrapped in soft musk
note: Bare Vanilla Cashmere is listed as vanilla orchid, plush patchouli and cosy skin musk. Vanilla absolute gives the real creamy vanilla, one drop of patchouli adds the plush, slightly earthy depth, sandalwood softens it, and a white musk fragrance oil gives the cosy finish. Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba, and let it rest a few days. Patch test first.

name: Berry meringue cashmere perfume oil (like Victoria's Secret Pure Seduction Cashmere)
claim: Juicy red berries over whipped, creamy sweetness
note: Listed notes: decadent red berries, whipped meringue and powdery cream. Berry and meringue have no natural oils, so they come from skin-safe fragrance oils (a red berry or plum one, and a meringue, marshmallow or whipped cream one); vanilla and musk make it soft and "cashmere". Geranium adds a rosy-fruity lift. Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba and rest a few days. Patch test.

name: Spun sugar petals cashmere perfume oil (like Victoria's Secret Velvet Petals Cashmere)
claim: Soft petals, toasted spun sugar and blonde woods
note: Listed notes: pillowy petals, toasted spun sugar and soft blonde woods. Rose and a touch of jasmine give the petals; a cotton candy or caramel fragrance oil gives the spun sugar; cedarwood and sandalwood are the "blonde woods". Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba and rest a few days. Patch test.

name: Nectarine marshmallow cashmere perfume oil (like Victoria's Secret Love Spell Cashmere)
claim: Ripe nectarine and peach over fluffy marshmallow and amber
note: Listed notes: ripe nectarine, fluffy marshmallow, peach musk and amber. Fruit and marshmallow are fragrance-oil notes (a peach or nectarine one plus a marshmallow one); vanilla stands in for amber, and musk keeps it soft. Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba and rest a few days. Patch test.

name: Cashmere-style body mist (any scent in the collection)
claim: A light, cosy mist like the Victoria's Secret Cashmere mists
note: Victoria's Secret mists are mostly water, alcohol, fragrance, glycerin, aloe and chamomile. This is the alcohol-free home version. Mix the fragrance oil with the polysorbate first (this lets it blend into water), then add the water, aloe, glycerin and chamomile hydrosol, and the preservative last. Use one blend from any Cashmere perfume oil above, or a ready-made fragrance oil; keep it to about 2% of the bottle. Shake before each use. Mists fade fast; layer over the matching perfume oil, or over an unscented lotion, to make it last.

name: VS-style body mist, alcohol base (clear, store-like)
claim: A crisp, clear mist like the Victoria's Secret bottles
note: The method soap suppliers and Victoria's Secret use: fragrance oil dissolved in perfumer's alcohol, so it never separates or clogs the sprayer. Weigh the fragrance oil into a clean glass beaker, add the alcohol, stir for a minute, and funnel it into a glass spray bottle. Rest it in a dark cupboard for at least 2 days (up to 2 weeks) so the alcohol smell softens. 4% fragrance is a typical body mist; check your oil's IFRA certificate for the hydroalcoholic body spray limit (Category 4). For a Cashmere dupe, use a marshmallow or vanilla cashmere fragrance oil and add 1 drop of patchouli (Bare Vanilla), a berry oil (Pure Seduction) or a brown sugar oil (Velvet Petals). Sizes: 50 g batch = 2 g fragrance + 48 g alcohol; 200 g = 8 g + 192 g. Flammable while mixing; keep away from flames.

name: Cashmere-style eau de parfum (15%, longer lasting)
claim: A stronger spray perfume, not a mist
note: Eau de parfum strength: 15% fragrance oil with a little distilled water to soften the first alcohol blast. Mix the oil into the alcohol first, then add the water. Store in glass with a fine-mist pump, rest it 2 weeks, and shake if it turns slightly cloudy. Spray 1 to 3 times on clothes or pulse points, not over large areas: this is a lot of fragrance on skin, so check that 15% is within your oil's IFRA limit and patch test. 50 g batch: 7.5 g oil, 2.5 g water, 40 g alcohol.

name: Coat pocket tallow balm (as posted)
claim: Simple balm for cold days and extra nourishment
note: As posted: tallow, calendula-infused jojoba, beeswax and castor oil, melted gently, then vitamin E stirred in and poured into small glass jars. A good, water-free winter balm for hands, knuckles, lips and dry patches. Tallow is rich and can clog pores on the face for some people; on hands and body it's great. Use rendered, cosmetic-grade or well-filtered tallow, or it smells beefy. Keeps about 6 to 12 months cool and dry.

name: Vegan winter pocket balm (no tallow)
claim: Same protective balm, plant-based and less pore-clogging
note: Shea and a little cocoa replace the tallow, so it's vegan and gentler for breakout-prone skin. Melt the beeswax and butters in a water bath, add the oils off the heat, then vitamin E, and pour into small tins. Swap the beeswax for 8 g candelilla wax to make it fully vegan.

name: Vanilla almond cocoa body butter (real vanilla bean)
claim: Whipped body butter speckled with real vanilla
note: Like the viral fall body butters: cocoa and shea butters with sweet almond oil, scraped vanilla bean seeds for the speckles, and a little vanilla absolute for scent (vanilla seeds alone smell faint). Melt the butters, stir in the almond oil and vanilla seeds, chill until the edges set (about 30 minutes), add the absolute and vitamin E, then whip 5 minutes until fluffy. Contains nuts. Cocoa butter smells like chocolate on its own, which pairs well with vanilla.

name: Strong-hold curl defining gel (flaxseed, for 4C)
claim: Thick, creamy hold that defines curls and reduces shrinkage
note: How products like Curlcombo get definition on 4C hair: a thick gel with strong hold, applied to soaking-wet hair in small sections, then left to dry without touching. Simmer whole flaxseed in water 8 to 10 minutes until it drips like egg white, strain hot through a stocking, cool, then stir in the aloe, a little glycerin and the preservative. Without the preservative it spoils in days. Glycerin: in very dry winter air or very humid weather it can make hair frizzy or sticky, so leave it out then. Low-porosity hair: use less, on wet hair, and skip heavy butters on top. Fine, low-density hair gets the most definition with a lighter amount; clumping with lots of product can make the scalp look sparse.

name: Spicy rose perfume oil (like Mallee Rose Burn)
note: Rose Burn by Australian niche brand Mallee is described as a spicy, grounded rose that isn't too dark. Rose and geranium give the rose, pink-ish pepper and cardamom the spice, and patchouli and sandalwood ground it. Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba, and rest a week. Patch test.

name: Hyaluronic hydrating face mist (like Rellet)
claim: Fine mist that hydrates in seconds
note: Rellet's viral HA spray is basically water, glycerin and sodium hyaluronate in a fine-mist can. Dissolve the hyaluronic acid in the water (stir and leave 30 minutes), add the rest, preservative last. Mist and press in, then follow straight away with moisturiser; on its own, in dry air, water evaporates and can leave skin feeling tighter.

name: Korean rice cream hair mask (as posted, blended rice)
claim: Thick rice "cream" mask for stronger, softer hair
note: The viral rice cream: cooked rice blended with water (and often a spoon of oil) until smooth, then strained through a cloth so no grains stay in the hair. Apply to damp, clean hair, leave 20 to 30 minutes, and rinse very well, then condition. It's starch and a little protein: it can make hair feel thicker and smoother for a while. Use once every 1 to 2 weeks. Like rice water, it can leave low-porosity or protein-sensitive hair stiff and brittle; one commenter says rice water made her hair break badly, and that does happen. If hair feels hard or snaps after, stop and do a moisturising mask instead. Make fresh and use the same day.

name: Conditioner bar (pairs with a shampoo bar)
claim: Solid conditioner that detangles and softens
note: Shampoo and conditioner bars go together; this is the conditioner half. BTMS is the conditioning, detangling ingredient in most solid conditioners. Melt the BTMS, cetearyl alcohol and butters in a water bath, take off the heat, stir in the oil and panthenol, then pour into a mould and let it set. To use: after shampoo, glide the bar over wet lengths a few times, work it through, and rinse. Keep it dry between uses.

name: Bergamot sandalwood perfume oil (like The 7 Virtues)
note: The 7 Virtues' bergamot and sandalwood scent. Bergamot FCF gives the sparkle without sunlight burns; a touch of sweet orange brightens it; sandalwood and a little vanilla give the soft, warm base. Mix in a 10 ml roller, top up with jojoba and rest a few days. "Aromatherapy you can wear" is a mood claim: pleasant scents can lift mood a little, nothing more.

name: Jasmine white tea scented shampoo (like KONO)
claim: Shampoo that leaves hair smelling like perfume
note: KONO-style "perfume shampoos" are ordinary shampoos with a lot of fragrance. Start with an unscented, sulfate-free shampoo base and stir in a skin-safe jasmine or white tea fragrance oil at 0.5 to 1%. More than that won't last 48 hours either; scent on hair mostly comes from the conditioner or a hair mist left on. Fragrance on the scalp can irritate, so keep it low.

name: Sleep well bath soak (like Sahajan)
note: Close to Sahajan's listed formula: Epsom and Dead Sea salts, baking soda and citric acid (a gentle fizz), kaolin clay, almond, sacha inchi and jojoba oils, a mild foaming powder that helps the oils spread, and lavender, nutmeg, tangerine, sandalwood and jasmine. Whisk the dry ingredients, rub the oils and scent in with your fingertips until it looks like damp sand, and store in a dry, airtight jar. This makes about 2 baths. Use about half a cup in warm running water and soak 20 minutes. What's real: warm water and a calming scent help you wind down; oils soften skin. Not real: "detoxifying" and "remineralising"; skin doesn't absorb meaningful minerals from a bath. Oils make the tub slippery, so step out carefully.

name: Japanese hot-spring bath powder (like Matsukiyo / Bathclin)
claim: Onsen-style bath that feels warmer for longer
note: Japanese medicated bath powders are mostly sodium sulfate and sodium bicarbonate, the salts found in many hot springs, plus a humectant (trehalose) and scent. They're sold as "quasi-drugs" in Japan for stiff shoulders, back aches and feeling cold. What's real: dissolved salts make the water feel silkier and slow the loss of warmth from skin after you get out, and a warm 15-minute bath does relax muscles. The salts themselves don't treat pain. Rub the oils into the polysorbate first, then stir it through the powder; store dry and airtight. Use 25 to 30 g (about 2 tablespoons) in a full tub (200 L) of 38 to 41 C water. Forest version: hinoki and cypress. Yuzu version: swap for sweet orange and a drop of grapefruit (fine in a rinse-off bath).

name: Japanese herbal bath sachet (yakuto, like Matsukiyo LAB)
claim: Warming herbal tea bath for cold legs and stiffness
note: Yakuto (薬草湯, medicinal herb bath) uses dried roots and leaves in a drip bag, like a big tea bag in the tub. Classic herbs: angelica root (toki), chamomile, ginger, citrus peel and mugwort; cnidium root is left out here, as it's hard to buy and can irritate. Fill a large muslin or paper tea bag, tie it, and drop it in while the tub fills; squeeze it a few times. Ginger and warm water make you feel warmer; the evidence for treating anything is traditional. Use each bag once. Skip ginger on broken skin, and skip mugwort and chamomile if you have a ragweed or daisy allergy.

name: Herbal tea bath bags (like Inoki)
note: Inoki's tea baths are blends of tea, flowers and herbs in large bags. Colloidal oatmeal is the one ingredient here with real proof: it's an approved skin protectant that eases itch and dryness. Fill a muslin bag, steep it in the tub as it fills, then squeeze it out. Use once and compost.

name: Kneipp-style aroma bath oil (dispersing)
claim: Herbal bath oil that blends into the water
note: Kneipp bath oils are a plant oil base (often soybean or almond) with an emulsifier, so the oil spreads through the water as a milky film instead of floating, plus essential oils. Stir together and use 1 to 2 capfuls (15 to 30 ml) in a full tub. Variants: Gute Nacht (good night): lavender with a drop of vetiver. Goodbye Stress: rosemary and a little peppermint (not in the evening). Almond blossom (Mandelblüten): leave out the essential oils entirely for dry, sensitive skin. Rinse the tub after; oils make it slippery.

name: Kneipp-style bath crystals
claim: Scented salt crystals for a herbal bath
note: Kneipp bath crystals are coarse brine salt with essential oils and a little emulsifier so the oil mixes into the water. Mix the polysorbate with the oils first, then stir into the salt until evenly coated. Use about 60 g (a small handful) per bath. Colour with a pinch of mica if you like.

name: Classic eau de cologne (like 4711)
note: The original eau de cologne: a light citrus and herb blend at about 3% in alcohol. 4711's style is bergamot, lemon, orange and neroli with a herbal touch of rosemary and lavender. Bergamot FCF and steam-distilled lemon won't burn skin in sun. Mix the oils into the alcohol, add the water, rest 2 weeks in a dark cupboard, then splash or spray. Fades in 1 to 2 hours, which is the point; it's a refresher. Flammable while mixing.

name: Zinc barrier cream for chafing (like Penaten, adult use)
claim: Thick protective cream for chafed, irritated skin
note: Penaten and similar European pharmacy creams are zinc oxide in a lanolin and petroleum-jelly base: zinc soothes and shields, lanolin holds moisture. This adult version is for chafing under the breasts, between thighs or on dry, cracked patches. Melt the lanolin, petrolatum and beeswax, then whisk in the zinc oxide until smooth (wear a mask while measuring powder) and stir until cool. Water-free, so no preservative. About 7% zinc, like the classic creams; it is not a sunscreen. For a baby's diaper rash, use a tested store cream; babies need products made and tested for them.

name: Sweet winter bath crystals (like Kneipp Süße Winterzeit)
claim: Cosy vanilla-tonka bath for cold days
note: Kneipp's winter sachets pair salt crystals with cosy notes (this one lists vanilla, pistachio and tonka). Tonka has no safe natural oil for skin, so vanilla plus a skin-safe tonka or pistachio fragrance oil gives the scent. Mix the oils into the polysorbate, then stir through the salt. Use about 60 g per bath.

name: Tamarind coffee glow scrub (like Pangju Formula 01)
claim: Thai-style polishing scrub for rough, dull skin
note: Pangju doesn't publish its full ingredient list; it says tamarind (a natural AHA), coffee and Thai herbs. Pangju says to massage gently, not scrub hard. This keeps-in-a-jar version uses dried tamarind powder, fine coffee and sugar in oil (fresh tamarind paste spoils in days). On damp skin, massage gently over rough spots (elbows, knees), leave 5 minutes, rinse. The quick rinse means the fruit acid does little; most of the smoothness is from the scrub and oil. 2 to 3 times a week, not on days you use glycolic or a retinoid on the body. Use a dry spoon; no water in the jar.

name: Chocolate glaze oil scrub (like Pangju Formula 02)
claim: Moisturising cocoa scrub for dry skin
note: Cocoa butter and oils with fine sugar and cocoa powder for colour and scent. Melt the cocoa butter, stir in the oils, cool, then mix in the sugar and cocoa. Massage 3 minutes on damp skin, leave 5, rinse. Gentle enough for more frequent use. Pangju's tip of mixing 01 and 02 works here too: half and half in your palm.

name: Strawberry skin night (glycolic + urea, the safe way)
claim: Smoother legs and fewer dark pores
note: The routine in the viral post works, just not all at once: glycolic 2 to 3 nights a week, a urea cream on the other nights, and a body retinol only after a month, never on the same night as glycolic. This is the urea cream half: 10% urea for KP and rough skin. Dissolve urea and glycerin in the water, heat with the oil phase to 70 C, blend, cool, then add the preservative. Shave or wax before, not right after, applying acids. Sunscreen on exposed legs.

name: Chamomile salve (as posted, Evergreen Apothecary)
claim: Soothing salve for dry, irritated skin and after sun
note: As posted: cover dried chamomile with jojoba for 2 to 6 weeks, strain well, then melt 1 cup infused oil with ¼ cup beeswax and 2 tbsp shea, and pour into tins. A good, water-free salve. Fine for dry patches and chapping; on scrapes, wash first and use a clean finger. Skip if allergic to ragweed or daisies. Don't put it on a fresh sunburn; cool the skin first, salve the next day.

name: Glycerin and baby oil body oil-lotion (student budget)
claim: Cheap, effective fix for very dry skin
note: The viral budget combo works: glycerin pulls water into skin and mineral (baby) oil seals it in, both cheap and among the best-studied moisturisers. Undiluted glycerin feels sticky and can even pull water out of skin in dry air, so mix it with water. Shake before use (it separates), rub into damp skin after a shower. Water means it needs a preservative, or make a week's worth and keep it in the fridge.

name: Lavender honey soap (like Earth to Body, melt and pour)
claim: Honeycomb soap with clay, cacao and shimmer
note: Melt the soap base gently, stir in honey (no more than 1 tsp per 100 g or it sweats), yellow clay (kaolin works) and a pinch of cacao, then lavender and a honey fragrance oil. Pour onto a honeycomb mat or mould. Manuka honey's wound-healing evidence is for medical-grade dressings; in soap it just adds a little lather and story. Activated charcoal is only for colour here. Wrap bars in cling film so they don't sweat.

name: Clean white musk body mist (like Ard Al Zaafaran Pure Musk)
note: Clean musks (white musk) are synthetic, not animal; they smell like warm, freshly washed skin and laundry. Use a white musk fragrance oil with a touch of lavender and rose for the soapy, powdery feel. Mix in perfumer's alcohol, rest 2 days. Spray on body and clothes. For hair, spray on a brush, not straight on, since alcohol dries ends.

name: Hair perfume mist (alcohol-light)
claim: Makes hair smell freshly washed all day
note: The creator's hair mist question in DIY form. Mostly water with a little glycerin and a solubilizer, so it doesn't dry your ends like alcohol perfumes. Mix the fragrance with the polysorbate first, then add the rest and the preservative. Mist lengths from 20 cm; avoid the scalp.

name: Mild clarifying shampoo (hard water and build-up)
note: Like ION or purifying shampoos. The easy DIY: a clear, sulfate-free shampoo with no oils or silicones, used generously with two lathers. For real hard-water build-up you need a chelator (disodium EDTA or sodium phytate, 0.2%), which is easiest to get in a store clarifying shampoo; don't add citric acid to castile soap, it turns it curdy. Use every 2 to 4 weeks, then condition well. Not a daily shampoo.

name: Vietnamese herbal body powder mask (like XUME bột thảo mộc)
claim: Weekly polishing body mask for smooth, glowing skin
note: XUME's label lists beetroot, rose, licorice, red bean, rice bran and oat powders; you mix a few spoons with unsweetened yogurt and leave it on ("ủ") before showering. Store the powder dry; only mix with yogurt when you use it. Spread over damp skin, leave 10 to 15 minutes, massage gently while rinsing, then moisturise. What it does: the powders polish off dull flakes and the yogurt's lactic acid softens, so skin looks smoother and brighter right away. The bright red is beetroot dye, not "whitening"; it can tint nails, towels and grout pink, and "dưỡng trắng" (whitening) results in the photos are lighting. Licorice has small studies for dark spots, but in a 15-minute rinse-off it does little. Once or twice a week.

name: Honey hair mask (for dry, brittle ends)
note: Honey is a humectant: it pulls water into hair. Mix with conditioner so it spreads and rinses out easily. Apply to damp lengths, leave 20 minutes under a shower cap, then rinse with warm water and condition. Any runny honey works; clover, wildflower or acacia are cheapest. Raw honey contains a tiny amount of hydrogen peroxide, which can lighten hair very slightly over many uses. Not for very humid days on fine hair (can feel sticky).

name: Honey blemish spot mask
note: Dab a tiny amount of manuka (or any raw honey) on one closed spot, cover with a pimple patch so it stays put, and rinse in the morning. Never on an open or picked spot; that needs a sterile, medical-grade honey dressing or a hydrocolloid patch. Small studies show honey calms inflammation; it won't replace benzoyl peroxide or adapalene for real acne.

name: Bridal ubtan body polish (as posted, 18 powders)
note: Your list as written: neem, licorice, gram flour, manjistha, red sandalwood, lodhra, mango turmeric, rose petal, rice flour, moong dal, sandalwood, orange peel, masoor dal, almond, chironji, mustard seed, camphor and saffron, mixed with water or rose water. Three of these need care: camphor and mustard seed can sting and irritate, especially over a large area and on freshly waxed or shaved skin; turmeric stains; and almond and chironji are nuts. A rinse-off ubtan with this many powders mostly works by polishing and softening, so the safer version below keeps the glow without the irritants. Keep the dry mix sealed; only add liquid when you use it.

name: Bridal ubtan body polish (gentler, wedding-safe)
claim: Soft, glowing skin before the big day
note: Same tradition, irritants out: no camphor or mustard seed, a little kasturi (wild) turmeric that stains less, and milk or yogurt instead of water for extra softness (rose water works too). Mix 2 to 3 tablespoons with liquid into a paste, spread on damp skin, let it dry for 10 minutes until slightly tacky (not cracking), then rub off in circles with wet hands and rinse. Twice a week in the month before the wedding; stop 2 days before mehndi so the henna takes evenly, and never on freshly waxed skin. Patch test on the inner arm 2 days ahead. Contains nuts (almond, chironji).

name: After-shave and ingrown oil (light, non-greasy)
claim: Calms razor burn and helps prevent ingrowns
note: The 4-step shave routine: shave butter, sharp razor, after-shave oil, ingrown oil. This oil does the last two in one. Squalane and jojoba sink in fast (it won't stain clothes once absorbed), and a little tea tree calms bumps. Press 3 to 4 drops into freshly shaved skin. Ingrowns are best prevented by a sharp blade, shaving with the grain, and a gentle exfoliant (lactic or salicylic acid lotion) 2 to 3 nights a week, on non-shave nights. If your thighs get hives and itch after shaving, that's razor irritation: try an electric trimmer, never dry shave, and skip fragranced products there.

name: Eczema cooling mist (fragrance-free)
claim: Calms itchy, tight patches between moisturiser layers
note: The creator's "eczema cooler" idea, made gentle: water, glycerin, panthenol and colloidal oatmeal extract, the one ingredient approved as a skin protectant for eczema itch. No essential oils, no fragrance, no witch hazel (all common eczema triggers). Mist, then seal straight away with a thick fragrance-free cream or balm, so the water doesn't evaporate and leave skin drier. Keep in the fridge for an extra cooling effect. For flares that bleed, weep or don't settle, see a doctor; short courses of prescribed creams are safe and stop the itch-scratch cycle.

name: Coffee licorice sugar scrub (Arabic Pangju-style, as posted)
claim: Coffee-chocolate polish with a creamy foam
note: From the comments: fine sugar, coffee grounds, licorice oil, wheat germ oil, almond oil and shower gel, softened with rose water. Lovely to use, but once you add shower gel and rose water it's a wet mix, so make one use at a time, or leave both out and add them in your palm each time. Licorice in a 5-minute rinse-off does little for dark spots; the glow is from the scrub and oils.

name: Vanilla brown sugar body scrub (THE SKINCARE QUEEN, measured)
note: Her list with measurements added (sugar = half raw cane, half brown): raw cane and brown sugar, coconut, argan, jojoba and avocado oils, vitamin E, and vanilla and almond extract. Swap kitchen extracts for vanilla absolute or a skin-safe fragrance oil: food extracts are mostly alcohol and water, which shorten shelf life and add little scent. No water in it, so it keeps 2 to 3 months if you scoop with a dry spoon; mould comes from wet hands in the jar, which is why some people get it and she doesn't. Glycerin does not stop mould (a commenter's tip); only a broad-spectrum preservative like Optiphen does, and only if the scrub contains water. Coconut oil firms up below 24 C, which can coat old drains; run hot water after. Epsom salt works instead of sugar but stings on fresh shaves.

name: Foaming vanilla poppy seed scrub (mariadelcarmencreates)
note: As posted: ⅓ cup whipped soap base, 1¼ cups sugar, 2 tbsp unscented castile soap, a few drops vanilla, 1 tsp vanilla bean powder, 1 tbsp almond oil, 1 tsp poppy seeds. Castile soap is mostly water, which is why she says 1 to 3 weeks without a preservative. This version drops the castile so the preserved whipped base is the only soap; it keeps much longer if you scoop with a dry spoon.

name: Curl combo (leave-in + flaxseed gel)
note: The "curl combo" is a leave-in cream topped with a gel. Use your favourite leave-in, then this preserved flaxseed-aloe gel on soaking-wet hair, in sections; let it dry without touching (it forms a soft cast you scrunch out). The ingredient "avoid" lists online are overstated: water-soluble silicones and mineral oil are fine for many coily heads if you clarify every few weeks; drying alcohols are the only real one to skip. Flaxseed gel vs African Pride: the gel defines more; African Pride's pre-poo detangles more. Use both if you like.

name: Oat, rice and chia slip hair mask with egg yolk (as posted)
note: Your recipe: blend oats, rice, chia seeds and (optional) dried hibiscus with warm water, strain through a fine cloth, then stir in egg yolk, argan and jojoba. The strained "milk" is starchy and slippery, which helps detangling; egg yolk adds fat and a little protein; the oils seal. Apply to damp hair, leave 20 to 30 minutes under a cap, rinse with cool or lukewarm water (hot water cooks the egg into bits), then a gentle shampoo or co-wash and conditioner. Hibiscus can tint very light or blonde hair pink. Make fresh and use the same day; don't store it.

name: Rosé petal mandelic body polish (like Olawunmi Allen)
claim: Silky, polished skin with a gentle acid
note: Her formula pairs a sugar polish with 3 to 5% mandelic acid, rose petals, chamomile and jojoba beads. Mandelic is the gentlest AHA and suits deeper skin, but in a polish you rinse off after a few minutes it does a little, not a lot. Water-free, so it keeps; scoop with a dry spoon. Massage gently on damp skin, rinse. Twice a week, not on scrub, retinoid or glycolic days, and not on freshly shaved or waxed skin.

name: Jamaican hot oil treatment (castor, aloe, honey)
claim: Grandma's remedy for dry hair and scalp
note: The Finance Baddie's recipe: Jamaican black castor oil, aloe vera ("sinkle bible") and honey. Warm the oil gently (warm to the wrist, never hot), stir in the aloe and honey, apply to scalp and lengths before washing, cover 20 to 30 minutes, then shampoo twice (castor is thick). It softens and seals; castor oil has no proof of growing hair, but less breakage means more length kept. Use once a week or two.

name: Yogurt coffee tahini mask for knees and elbows (Mear Ahmad)
claim: Softer, smoother dark knees and elbows
note: Her "دلكة تفتيح المفاصل" (joint-brightening paste): yogurt, Nescafé or Turkish coffee, oats and tahini, left to dry and rubbed off. It softens and polishes, so rough, dry knees and elbows look smoother and less ashy right away. It won't change your natural skin colour. Darker knees and elbows are mostly from friction and thicker skin; a urea or lactic acid lotion used daily is the leave-on fix. Make fresh. Contains sesame.

name: Gulf herbal soap paste (صابونية, Mear Ahmad Eid routine)
note: Her method: grate laurel (bay) soap and melt it in rose water, then mix in Moroccan black soap, sweet almond oil, ground wars and Turkish coffee; rest it a day, stir and use. It's a soft soap scrub: the soap cleanses, coffee polishes, and wars leaves a warm golden tint that reads as a "glow" (it's colour, not lightening). Soap is alkaline, but with this much rose water and coffee it can still spoil, so make enough for 1 to 2 uses (this amount) and keep it in the fridge between them; sellers' big jars need a preservative. Massage on damp skin 5 minutes, rinse, moisturise. Patch test the wars.

name: Coconut snow scrub (Mear Ahmad)
note: Her version: sugar, salt, starch or pearl powder, ground coconut, coconut oil, a coconut shower gel and chia seeds. This keeps-in-a-jar version leaves out the shower gel (add a squeeze in your palm when you use it) so no water gets in. Salt stings on fresh shaves; use sugar only then.

name: Sidr calming scrub (Mear Ahmad)
claim: Soothing herbal scrub, plus a sidr face wash
note: Sidr (jujube leaf) is the traditional Gulf herbal wash. Her scrub: sidr, sugar, under a quarter spoon of Turkish coffee, a tip of turmeric, jojoba oil, a spoon of aloe and shower gel; leave on dry skin 5 to 10 minutes while massaging. The second trick: shake a spoon of sidr in a bottle of water until it foams and thickens, then use the liquid as a gentle face and body wash; sidr's saponins lather lightly. Make the water version fresh each time. Turmeric stains; keep it to a pinch.

name: Easy chocolate coffee tamarind scrub (Mear Ahmad)
note: Her list: sugar, Turkish coffee, Nescafé, cocoa, Moroccan spice or any dried herbs, strained tamarind with Moroccan soap, shower gel and sweet or bitter almond oil. Use sweet almond, not bitter almond (bitter almonds can contain cyanide compounds). The tamarind and soap make it wet, so mix one use at a time. Skip hot spices like cinnamon or ginger in the herb mix; they sting.

name: Blue nila mask (like InayaMorocco)
claim: Brighter, smoother skin in a weekly mask
note: Nila is Moroccan indigo powder mixed with water or rose water. It's soothing and a little polishing, but most "brightening" in videos is the contrast after washing off dark blue. Buy pure Indigofera (much nila is synthetic dye), patch test, keep it off eyelids, and expect blue on nails, towels and grout. 5 to 10 minutes, then rinse and moisturise. Once a week.

name: Blended beauty bar (melting soaps together, the right way)
claim: Combine the bars you love into one
note: Grate finished bars, melt with a little water over simmering water until like mashed potatoes, press into a mould, unmould after 1 to 2 days and dry 1 to 2 weeks. Check every bar's label first in Can I mix these? → Blending products.

source.creator: Family tradition (cutting and mixing beauty soaps)

name: Enriched body cream (mixing creams the safe way)
claim: A richer version of the lotion you already use
note: Soften the shea, stir it into the lotion with the oil using a clean spoon, in a clean jar. No water, juice or fresh ingredients. Use within 4 weeks and throw out if it separates or smells off.

name: Sidr and gum arabic calming mask (like InayaMorocco)
claim: Antioxidants for tired-looking skin and a soothing film
note: Keep it off the eyelids and lash line: sidr foams and can sting eyes. Leave 10 minutes, rinse, then 2 drops of argan oil.

name: Gulf "brightening" soap paste (صابونية تفتيح), as posted
note: As posted: grate licorice soap, Dove, Pyary turmeric and Kojie San, cover with a whole bottle of rose water, leave 12 hours, then stir in 3 spoons of corn starch (optionally Kream Kap scrub cream) and keep it in a jar. With this much rose water and starch the jar can grow mould within a week or two. The soaps' kojic acid, licorice and turmeric touch skin for a minute, so it cleans and softens but won't lighten. See the safer version.

name: Gulf soap paste (صابونية), safer small batch
claim: A soft soap scrub for 3 to 4 showers
note: Grate the bars you like (check each one in Can I mix these? → Blending products first), soak in just enough rose water to soften, about 1 part rose water to 3 parts soap, overnight in the fridge. Stir in the starch, keep it in the fridge and use within 2 weeks; toss it if it smells sour or grows spots. Massage on damp skin for 2 to 3 minutes, rinse, moisturise. It cleans and polishes; for dark spots use a leave-on product.

source.creator: Safer version of the viral صابونية

name: Gulf soap paste, full haul version (inher66), as posted
note: As posted (amounts are our estimate): grated Dove, Kojie San, papaya, Tawoos and laurel soap and Pyary turmeric soap, with turmeric body powder, rose water, sweet and bitter almond oil, glycerin, rose oil, blue nila, "white henna", Herbolene aloe jelly, Glysolid and aker fassi for colour. Problems: bitter almond oil (use sweet), nila and aker fassi are often adulterated with dyes, "white henna" contents vary, and rose water plus cream in a big jar can spoil. Use the safer small batch instead.

name: Lemon scrub balls (Shima), as posted
note: As posted: mix everything except the starch, add starch until moldable, shape balls, dry 30 minutes, store airtight. Fresh zest and body wash bring water into a stored scrub, and cold-pressed lemon oil and zest can sun-sensitize. See the long-lasting version.

name: Lemon scrub balls that keep (no fresh zest)
note: Melt the coconut oil, stir in almond oil, vitamin E and lemon oil, then the sugar and starch until it holds when pressed. Shape, let firm 30 minutes, store dry with a dry spoon. Steam-distilled lemon oil isn't sun-sensitizing. Add a squirt of body wash to each ball in the shower instead of mixing it in.

name: Sidr and coconut milk hair mask
note: Mix into a smooth paste, apply to damp hair from roots to ends, leave 20 to 30 minutes, rinse well and condition. Sidr cleanses gently; coconut milk softens. Make it fresh each time.

name: Glysolid, aloe jelly and shea whip (Vlogger lama), as posted
claim: Deep moisture for very dry skin
note: As posted: whip Glysolid glycerin cream, Herbolene aloe petroleum jelly, organic shea, raw Ghana shea and sweet almond oil, then Johnson's baby oil. It works: shea and petroleum jelly seal moisture in, glycerin draws it in. But Glysolid is a water-based cream, so stretched into a big tub its preservative is diluted. Make small tubs and use within a month, or make it without the cream. Baby oil is mineral oil with fragrance: it seals moisture in, best on damp skin.

name: Shea and petroleum jelly body butter (keeps for months)
claim: The Glysolid whip, made to last
note: Melt the shea gently, stir in petroleum jelly and almond oil, cool until it starts to set, then whip until fluffy. No water means no mould. Apply on damp skin after a shower so it seals the water in. Use glycerin cream separately if you like it.

source.creator: Safer version of Vlogger lama's whip

name: Glycerin hand and body cream (Glysolid-style)
claim: Rich, non-greasy glycerin cream for hands, elbows and heels
note: Glysolid's work is done by water, glycerin and a simple emulsifier; its long perfume list is left out. Heat the water phase (water, glycerin, allantoin) and oil phase (Olivem, sunflower, shea) separately to 70°C, blend, cool below 40°C, stir in the preservative. Scale in grams; keeps about 6 months with Geogard. Fragrance-free, so it's gentler than the original.

name: Aloe petroleum jelly (Herbolene-style)
claim: Seals in moisture on dry skin, lips and heels
note: Herbolene is mineral oil and wax with a little aloe extract and perfume. Warm the petroleum jelly just until soft, stir in aloe oil and vitamin E, pour into a tin. No water, so it keeps for a year. Apply on damp skin.

source.creator: Dupe of Dabur Herbolene Aloe Jelly

name: Berry AHA body polish (Alina Tomato Berry scrub-style)
note: A gentle-acid polish built like the Rosé petal polish: mandelic acid (the mildest AHA) in an oil scrub that rinses milky. Beetroot gives the pink colour; tomato and berry extracts in the original are colour and story. Use 2 to 3 times a week on damp skin, not on freshly shaved skin, and cover up in the sun for a week after. Scoop with a dry spoon.

source.creator: Dupe of Alina Tomato Berry AHA Scrub

name: Creamy face and body scrub cream (Kream Kap-style)
claim: A soft exfoliating cream that rinses clean
note: Jojoba beads polish without scratching and don't dissolve in the cream (sugar and salt would). Make it like a lotion: heat water, glycerin and xanthan, and Olivem with sunflower, separately to 70°C, blend, cool below 40°C, add preservative, then fold in the beads. Gentle enough for the face once a week.

source.creator: Dupe of Kream Kap scrub cream

name: Rose facial cleansing bar (Sinkrose-style)
note: Melt the base, stir in rose water, rose powder and glycerin, add the rose oil just before pouring. The original's niacinamide is left out: in a soap it rinses away before it can do anything. Use a leave-on niacinamide serum if you want brightening.

source.creator: Dupe of SEÑO Sinkrose Facial Cleansing Soap

name: Seven-herb shampoo bar (Fuwari-style)
claim: Cleans the scalp with the same herbs
note: Uses the Fuwari herbs (rosemary, butterfly pea, ginseng, ginger, horsetail) in a melt-and-pour shampoo base. Grind the herbs finely so they rinse out. It's a pleasant herbal shampoo, but no shampoo regrows hair; for thinning, minoxidil is the proven option.

name: Green tea herbal scrub mask (Madame Aura-style)
claim: A gentle polish and calm, fresh-looking skin
note: Mix to a soft paste, smooth on, leave 10 minutes, then rub in small circles as you rinse. Rice flour is the gentle scrub; green tea and honey are soothing; turmeric is a pinch for colour (it stains). Once or twice a week. Make it fresh.

source.creator: Dupe of Madame Aura green tea scrub

name: Thai herbal mask powder (Kanchana-style)
note: Keep the dry powder in a dry jar (it lasts months). For each mask, mix 2 teaspoons with rose water or plain water, apply, rinse after 10 minutes, before it cracks. The bergamot (makrut) peel some Thai masks use is left out: it can cause burns and dark patches when skin then sees sun.

name: Perfumed body oil (Janua Forget Me Not-style)
claim: Soft, glowing skin that smells like your perfume
note: Stir the fragrance into the oils and let it sit 2 days so the scent settles. Use a skin-safe fragrance oil at no more than 1 to 2%, or 10 to 15 drops of your favourite perfume per 100 ml. Apply to damp skin after a shower; it smooths rough skin by sealing moisture in.

source.creator: Dupe of Janua perfumed body oil

name: Serum body milk (NIVEA Serum Burst Milk-style)
claim: A light, fast-absorbing body lotion for dry skin
note: Glycerin, niacinamide and panthenol in a thin lotion. Heat water, glycerin, panthenol and xanthan, and Olivem with sunflower, separately to 70°C, blend, cool below 40°C, then stir in the niacinamide (dissolved in a little water) and the preservative. Helps dry, flaky skin; no lotion removes stretch marks.

source.creator: Dupe of NIVEA Serum Burst Milk

name: Moroccan tbrima rubbing blend (Skalli Essentials-style)
claim: A softening herbal polish for the hammam shower
note: Mix the dry powders and keep in a dry jar (lasts months). For each use, wet a handful with rose water into a paste, rub over damp skin after the black soap, rinse. The original uses aker fassi for colour; it's left out because it's often cut with dyes. Body, or gently on the face once a week.

name: Nila and ghassoul mask (Skalli Essentials)
note: Mix ghassoul and a pinch of pure nila with rose water to a smooth paste, apply, rinse after 10 minutes before it cracks. Nila stains: test on your inner arm first and buy pure nila, not dyed powder.

name: Blended rice, tea and SA cleanser scrub (linnacheung7), as posted
note: As revealed in her comments: coarsely blended rice, the contents of 2 fruit tea bags, Cetaphil Gentle Exfoliating SA Cleanser and an oil, mixed into a jar. Two problems: the cleanser is mostly water, so a jar can grow mould in a wet shower; and stacking salicylic acid with a rice scrub daily is a lot of exfoliation (one commenter broke out). Also, rice grains can collect in drains. See the safer version.

name: Rice and tea body scrub (keeps, drain-friendly)
claim: The same soft skin, without mould
note: Mix the ground rice, tea leaves (from a bag) and oil in a dry jar; it keeps for months because there's no water. In the shower, take a scoop and add a squirt of your SA or gentle wash in your palm. Grind rice to coarse sand, not whole grains, and run hot water after to keep drains clear. 2 to 3 times a week.

name: In-shower body salve (hanni Splash Salve-style)
claim: Soft, moisturized skin straight out of the shower
note: Melt the shea and wax gently, stir in the oils and emulsifier, cool and whip. Polysorbate 80 lets it rinse off milky so only a thin layer stays. At the end of your shower, turn off the water, smooth a scoop over wet skin, rinse lightly, pat dry. No water inside, so it keeps for months; keep water out of the jar.

name: Taif rose sugar scrub (Miss White-style)
claim: A rose-scented polish for soft, glowing skin
note: Mix the dry ingredients, stir in the oils, scoop with a dry spoon. Beetroot powder gives the red colour (the original is likely dyed). It polishes and leaves skin soft and fragrant; it won't lighten skin. 2 to 3 times a week, not on freshly shaved skin.

source.creator: Dupe of Miss White Taif Rose Scrub

name: Moroccan nila sugar scrub (Miss White-style)
note: Mix dry, then add the oils; scoop with a dry spoon. Pure nila is used in a pinch for colour: much of what's sold is cut with synthetic blue dye, so buy from a seller who lists it as pure indigo and patch test. Nila doesn't lighten skin; any glow is from exfoliating. It can tint grout and towels.

name: Light body milk (Hatomugi-style)
claim: A watery, fast-absorbing body milk for daily moisture
note: Hatomugi's coix seed (Job's tears) extract is a mild soothing extract; colloidal oats do a similar, better-studied job. Heat water, glycerin, panthenol and xanthan, and Olivem with sunflower, to 70°C, blend, cool below 40°C, stir in the finely ground colloidal oats and preservative. Very light, like the original.
